blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 8 (Physical Optics and Gravitational Waves), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is meant by polarization of light? Explain with the example of transverse waves on a string why only transverse waves can be polarized, and describe how unpolarized light can be made polarized. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Wave nature: Interference and diffraction prove the wave nature of light but do not tell whether light waves are longitudinal or transverse. Polarization suggests that light waves are transverse.

Transverse waves on a string (Fig. 8.1): The particles of the medium vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation. The vibrations can be vertical, horizontal or along any other direction; in each case the wave is said to be polarized. The plane of polarization is the plane containing the direction of vibration and the direction of propagation.

Light: A light wave produced by an oscillating charge is a periodic variation of the electric field vector E accompanied by the magnetic field vector B, at right angle to each other. Ordinary light has components of vibration in all possible planes; it is unpolarized (e.g. sunlight, incandescent and fluorescent bulbs, candle, fire). If the vibrations are confined to one plane, the light is polarized.

Polarization: the process by which the electric and magnetic vibrations of light are restricted to a single plane of vibration. It is shown by transverse waves only; it does not occur for longitudinal waves such as sound, whose vibrations are along the direction of travel.

Methods of polarizing unpolarized light: (1) a polarizing filter such as a polaroid sheet; (2) a polarizing beam splitter; (3) optical crystals such as calcite and quartz. In a polarizing filter only the electric field vector parallel to the axis of the filter passes; all other vectors are blocked, so the emerging light is polarized (Fig. 8.3).

Basis: the orientation of the electric field vector E in a specific direction is the basis of polarization.

book_ref.quote: A light wave produced by oscillating charge consists of a periodic variation of the electric field vector

blocks.prompt: 2 Polarized light of amplitude 20 units falls on a polarizing filter whose axis makes 53° with the light's plane of vibration. Find the amplitude of the light that passes, and the fraction of the intensity transmitted. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Only the component of E along the filter's axis passes: A = A₀cos θ; intensity goes as the square of amplitude.

book_ref.quote: only that electric field vector which is parallel to the axis of polarized filter

blocks.final_answer: A = 12.0 units; about 36% of the intensity is transmitted

blocks.prompt: 3 Classify the polarization of light. Describe linear, circular and elliptical polarization with one example of each. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Light can be polarized in three basic ways, according to the path traced by the electric field vector E.

1. Linear polarization (Fig. 8.4 a): The electric field vector oscillates in a single plane. Example: light passing through a polarizing filter, like sunglasses.

2. Circular polarization (Fig. 8.4 b): The electric field rotates circularly, either clockwise (right-handed) or counterclockwise (left-handed). Example: light reflected off a CD (Compact Disc) or DVD (Digital Versatile Disc).

3. Elliptical polarization (Fig. 8.4 c): A combination of linear and circular polarization in which the electric field vector traces an elliptical path. The two components of the electric field, Ex and Ey, are not equal and/or they differ in phase by an arbitrary angle θ. Example: light passing through a stress plate or a waveplate.

book_ref.quote: Here are the basic types of polarization of light.

blocks.prompt: 4 Linearly polarized light falls on an analyzer. Through what angle must the analyzer's axis be turned from the plane of vibration so that the transmitted amplitude is 0.9 of the incident amplitude? What fraction of the intensity then passes? (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use A = A₀cos θ for the angle, then I/I₀ = (A/A₀)².

book_ref.quote: When the electric field vector oscillates in a single plane

blocks.prompt: 5 How can plane polarized light be produced and detected using two polaroids? Explain what this experiment proves about the nature of light. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Unpolarized source: Light emitted by an ordinary incandescent bulb (and by the Sun) is unpolarized because its electrical vibrations are randomly oriented in space (Fig. 8.5).

Production: When unpolarized light falls on a sheet of polaroid (the polarizer), the transmitted light is plane polarized.

Detection: A second polaroid (the analyzer) is placed in the beam.
• When the axes of the two polaroids (lines drawn on them) are parallel, the light is transmitted through the second polaroid (Fig. 8.5 a).
• When the analyzer is slowly rotated about the beam as axis, the emerging light gets dimmer and dimmer and disappears when the axes become mutually perpendicular (Fig. 8.5 b).
• On further rotation the light reappears and becomes brightest when the axes are again parallel.

What it proves: Light waves are transverse. If light waves were longitudinal, their vibrations would be along the direction of travel and the light would never disappear, even with the two polaroids mutually perpendicular.

book_ref.quote: If unpolarized light is made incident on a sheet of polaroid (polarizer), the transmitted light will be plane polarized.

blocks.prompt: 6 Plane polarized light of intensity 80 W m⁻² leaves a polarizer. Find the intensity passing through the analyzer when the angle between their axes is (i) 0° (ii) 30° (iii) 60° (iv) 90°. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Apply I = I₀cos²θ for each angle; the light should fade to zero at 90°, as in the experiment.

book_ref.quote: The light reappears on further rotation and becomes brightest when the axes are again parallel to each other.

blocks.final_answer: 80 W m⁻², 60 W m⁻², 20 W m⁻² and 0 (light extinguished at 90°)

blocks.prompt: 7 What is the polarizing angle? State and derive Brewster's law. What form does it take when the first medium is air? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Polarizing angle: The particular angle of incidence on a transparent medium at which the reflected light is almost plane polarized.

Derivation: Let a beam of unpolarized light fall on the surface of medium 2 from medium 1 (Fig. 8.6). When the reflected beam is almost plane polarized, i.e. at i = θp, the reflected and refracted beams are at right angle to each other. Thus
θp + θr = 90°
or θr = 90° − θp

From Snell's law:
n1 sin θp = n2 sin θr
n1 sin θp = n2 sin(90° − θp)
n1 sin θp = n2 cos θp
sin θp / cos θp = n2/n1
tan θp = n2/n1
This is Brewster's law; n1 and n2 are the refractive indices of media 1 and 2.

Medium 1 is air: n1 = 1 and n2 = n, so tan θp = n. The tangent of the polarizing angle is numerically equal to the refractive index of medium 2. The angle θp, at which the reflected and refracted rays make 90° between them, is also called the Brewster angle θB: tan θB = n.

book_ref.quote: Let a beam of unpolarized light be made incident on the surface of medium 2

blocks.prompt: 8 Light in air falls on a transparent plastic of refractive index 1.65 at the polarizing angle. Find (i) the polarizing angle (ii) the angle of refraction, and check the answer with Snell's law. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use tan θp = n, then θr = 90° − θp; Snell's law sin θp = n sin θr must hold.

book_ref.quote: A beam of light strikes the surface of a plate of glass with a refractive index

blocks.prompt: 9 How can polarized light be obtained by reflection? Describe Malus's observation and explain how a polaroid shows that reflected light is plane or partially polarized. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Discovery: In 1808 Malus discovered that polarized light is obtained when ordinary light is reflected (bounces back) from a plane sheet of glass.

Observation: The reflected light is viewed through a polaroid which is slowly rotated about the line of vision. At one position of the polaroid the light is practically extinguished. This proves that light reflected by the glass is practically plane polarized.

Best angle: The most suitable angle of incidence for glass is about 57°; at this angle the reflected ray becomes plane polarized (Fig. 8.6). This is the polarizing angle, at which the reflected and refracted rays are at 90° (Brewster's law, tan θp = n). The reflected light is polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence (shown by dots).

Partial polarization: Light reflected from the surface of a table becomes darker when viewed through a rotated polaroid, showing that it is partially plane polarized. Similarly, light reflected from the smooth surface of water is partially polarized parallel to the surface.

book_ref.quote: In 1808, Malus discovered that polarized light is obtained when ordinary light is reflected

blocks.prompt: 10 Light travelling in water (refractive index 1.33) is reflected from the surface of a glass block (refractive index 1.5) placed in the water. Find the polarizing angle and the angle of refraction. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Medium 1 is water, not air, so use the full form tan θp = n2/n1.

book_ref.quote: In this equation, n₁ is refractive index of medium 1

blocks.prompt: 11 What is optical activity? Give examples of optically active substances, the factors on which the rotation depends, its cause, and one use of it. (5 marks)

book_ref.quote: Many crystals and solutions rotate the plane of polarization of light passing through them.

blocks.prompt: 12 Polarized light of intensity 100 W m⁻² passes through a sugar solution that rotates its plane of polarization by 25°. The analyzer is kept with its axis parallel to the original plane of polarization. Find the intensity passing through the analyzer, and the angle through which the analyzer must be turned to get the maximum intensity. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: After the solution, the light's plane makes 25° with the analyzer's axis, so apply Malus's law with θ = 25°.

book_ref.quote: so that it is no longer horizontal but at an angle

steps: I₀ = 100 W m⁻², angle between plane of polarization and analyzer axis θ = 25°
Maximum intensity (I = I₀) needs θ = 0°, so the analyzer must be turned through 25° in the direction of rotation
blocks.final_answer: I = 82.1 W m⁻²; turn the analyzer through 25°

blocks.prompt: 13 State Malus's law. Derive the relation I = I₀cos²θ and discuss its two extreme conditions. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Statement: The intensity I of plane polarized light after passing through an analyzer is directly proportional to the square of the cosine of the angle θ between the transmission axes of the analyzer and the polarizer:
I ∝ cos²θ, or I = I₀cos²θ
where I₀ is the intensity of the incident polarized light (after passing through the polarizer), Fig. 8.7(a). An analyzer is also a polarizer placed after a polarizer; rotating it changes the transmitted intensity.

Derivation: Let polarized light of amplitude A₀ strike the analyzer, whose axis makes angle θ with the plane of polarization. A₀ is resolved into two components (Fig. 8.7 b):
A₀cos θ along the axis of the analyzer, and A₀sin θ perpendicular to it.
The component A₀sin θ is absorbed in the analyzer; only A₀cos θ passes. So the transmitted amplitude is
A = A₀cos θ
Intensity is the square of the amplitude:
I = A²
or I = A₀²cos²θ
I = I₀cos²θ (∵ I₀ = A₀²)

Extreme conditions:
• θ = 0°: I = I₀. The intensity through the analyzer equals the intensity that passes through the polarizer.
• θ = 90°: I = 0. The light is extinguished completely; no light passes through the analyzer.

book_ref.quote: When the incident polarized light of amplitude A₀ strikes the analyzer at an angle

blocks.prompt: 14 The intensity of polarized light is to be reduced by 70% using an analyzer. Find the angle between the axes of polarizer and analyzer, and the fraction of the amplitude transmitted. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: A 70% reduction leaves I = 0.30 I₀; solve I = I₀cos²θ for θ, and A/A₀ = cos θ.

book_ref.quote: It is used to further reduce the intensity of light and also adjust it

blocks.final_answer: θ = 56.8°; about 0.55 of the amplitude is transmitted

blocks.prompt: 15 What is a polaroid? Explain the two main applications of polarizers, and list the importance of polarization in other fields. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Polaroid: Certain transparent crystalline materials, like tourmaline and calcite, confine the vibrations of light waves to only one plane. Such materials, with high directionality in crystal structure, are called polaroids. Light can also be polarized naturally by reflection, refraction and scattering.

1. Sky photography: A camera used to photograph the clouds is fitted with a polaroid. Polarizers reduce the glare and haze produced by scattering of light by small particles in the atmosphere. They enhance contrast by blocking excessive bright white light while allowing other colours to pass, giving a brighter, detailed image and better overall quality.

2. Stress analysis of materials: Polarizers are used to analyze stress and strain in plastics, metals and glass. When a material is stressed its molecular structure changes, affecting its interaction with light, and interference fringes are formed. By shining polarized light through the transparent material and analysing changes in polarization, researchers can determine stress patterns, identify weaknesses or defects, analyze optical properties and understand behaviour under different conditions. This technique is called photoelasticity, used in engineering, materials science and quality control.

Importance in other fields: optics and photonics (polarized sunglasses, LCD screens, optical communication); imaging and microscopy (reducing glare, improving contrast); medicine (cancer diagnosis, tissue imaging, laser surgery); astronomy (light from distant stars, cosmic microwave background radiation).

book_ref.quote: In both cases described above, polarizers play a crucial role

blocks.prompt: 16 Polarized light from part of the sky reaches a camera polaroid with intensity 150 W m⁻². (i) What intensity passes when the polaroid's axis is at 50° to the plane of polarization? (ii) At what angle would 120 W m⁻² pass? (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The camera polaroid acts as an analyzer: use I = I₀cos²θ both ways.

book_ref.quote: The light coming from the sky is polarized by the polaroid.

blocks.prompt: 17 What are gravitational waves? Explain them with the pond analogy and describe their four basic types. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of spacetime, produced by violent cosmic events like colliding black holes or neutron stars, that travel at the speed of light carrying information about their source. A gravitational wave is a stretching and compressing of space, observed by measuring the change in length between two objects.

Pond analogy: A stone thrown into a pond creates ripples on the water surface (spacetime). The ripples travel outward carrying information about the stone (the cosmic event) and can be detected on the shore (by gravitational wave observatories).

Four basic types:
1. Continuous GWs: produced when a single massive object, such as a neutron star, spins at a constant rate; same frequency and amplitude. White dwarf binary systems also produce continuous GWs.
2. Compact binary inspiral GWs: produced by a binary system, such as binary neutron stars, binary black holes, or a neutron star and a black hole orbiting each other.
3. Burst GWs: produced by violent events like supernovae, gamma-ray bursts or cosmic strings.
4. Stochastic GWs: weak, random signals produced by the superposition of many weak sources such as distant binary systems; the most difficult to detect.

Every accelerating object produces GWs, but masses and accelerations on the Earth (vehicles, airplanes) are too small to give detectable waves.

book_ref.quote: There are four basic types of gravitational waves, each with different sources and characteristics:

blocks.prompt: 18 Taking the speed of gravitational waves as c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, find (i) the frequency of gravitational waves of wavelength 1200 km (ii) the wavelength of gravitational waves of frequency 150 Hz. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: GWs move with the speed of light, so v = fλ becomes c = fλ.

book_ref.quote: that travel at the speed of light, carrying information about their source

blocks.prompt: 19 Explain how Einstein's general theory of relativity describes gravity and predicts gravitational waves. What is spacetime distortion (tidal forces), and why is it so hard to detect at the Earth? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Gravity in general relativity: Gravity is not a force but a curvature of spacetime caused by massive bodies. Like a dent in a mattress, heavy things warp the space around them, and that is why we feel gravity. Gravitational waves are a prediction of this theory (Einstein, 1916), now confirmed by observation; they were first detected on 14 September 2015, from two merging black holes.

Sources: A binary system, two compact objects (black holes, neutron stars or white dwarfs) orbiting each other, emits GWs. As the masses orbit and accelerate, their gravitational intensity fluctuates and waves radiate outward in all directions at the speed of light, weakening as they move away. Their characteristics depend on the masses, the orbital period and frequency, and the eccentricity of the orbit.

Spacetime distortion (tidal forces): A GW passing through a body with mass makes the spacetime around it oscillate, so the body is periodically stretched and compressed in the direction perpendicular to the wave's propagation. This is similar to the tides on Earth caused by the Moon and Sun. The amount depends on the strength of the wave and the mass and size of the body.

Why hard to detect: The amplitude of GWs reaching the Earth is a strain ΔL/L of only about 10⁻²¹ to 10⁻²² (no unit). For LIGO's 4 km arms this is a change of about 10⁻¹⁸ m, so extremely sensitive instruments are needed. Even so, GWs let us study strong-field gravity, test general relativity and explore the universe in new ways.

book_ref.quote: As the gravitational wave passes through the body, it causes the spacetime around the body to oscillate

blocks.prompt: 20 A gravitational wave of strain ΔL/L = 5 × 10⁻²² passes through the Earth. Find the change in length of (i) a LIGO arm of 4 km (ii) a Virgo arm of 3 km. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Strain is the fractional change in length, so ΔL = strain × L, with L in metres.

book_ref.quote: For LIGO's 4 km arms such a wave changes the arm length

blocks.prompt: 21 What is an interferometer? Describe the basic components of a gravitational wave interferometer and explain how it detects a gravitational wave. How does LIGO differ from a conventional interferometer? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: An interferometer is an optical tool used in detecting gravitational waves. It is a very sensitive device that may use the interference of LASER beams; the basic Michelson's interferometer is shown in Fig. 8.9. A GW interferometer uses LASER light to measure tiny changes in distance between mirrors caused by gravitational waves passing through it.

Basic components:
• Laser: produces a stable, high intensity beam of light.
• Power recycling mirror: continually reflects LASER light that has already travelled through the instrument back into the interferometer.
• Beam splitter: divides the LASER beam into two perpendicular beams.
• Mirrors: reflect the beams, creating two perpendicular arms.
• Fabry Perot cavity: two mirrors facing each other, to enhance the path length.
• Arm cavities: enhance the LASER light, increasing sensitivity.
• Photodetectors: measure the returning beams, detecting tiny phase shifts.

Working: The laser beam is split into two perpendicular beams travelling down two identical arms. They bounce off the mirrors at the ends and return to be recombined, creating an interference pattern measured by a photodetector. A passing GW causes a tiny disturbance in the distance between the mirrors, producing a phase shift between the beams; this alters the interference pattern, so the detector senses the wave.

LIGO vs conventional: LIGO is 1000 times larger than a conventional device, and LIGO uses a LASER whereas a conventional interferometer has a normal light source.

book_ref.quote: An interferometer that detects gravitational waves is a highly sensitive instrument

blocks.prompt: 22 A LIGO arm is 4 km long. (i) If LIGO is 1000 times larger than a conventional interferometer, estimate the arm length of the conventional device. (ii) Find the time taken by laser light (speed 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) to travel down one LIGO arm and back once. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Divide by 1000 for the size; for the time, the light covers 2L at speed c, so t = 2L/c.

book_ref.quote: LIGO is 1000 times larger than conventional device

steps: (ii) Distance down and back = 2L = 2 × 4000 m = 8000 m

blocks.prompt: 23 Describe the Virgo gravitational wave observatory and compare it with LIGO. Also give an account of the first observation of gravitational waves. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Virgo: Similar to LIGO, Virgo is another facility for measuring gravitational waves. It works under the European Gravitational Observatory (EGO) at Cascina near Pisa, Italy. It is an interferometer with two arms of 3 km, whereas LIGO (in the USA) has 4 km arms. It is named after the Virgo constellation, visible in the night sky in March, April and May. The Virgo cluster is a group of about 1,500 galaxies about 50 million light years away; one light year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 × 10¹² km. Virgo made its first detection of a gravitational wave event in 2017.

First observation: On 14 September 2015, gravitational waves were observed for the very first time by LIGO. These waves, predicted by Albert Einstein 100 years earlier, came from a collision between two black holes and took 1.3 billion years to reach the LIGO detector in the USA. For this work Rainer Weiss, Barry C. Barish and Kip S. Thorne received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2017. One of the team members, Professor Nergis Mavalvala of MIT, belongs to Pakistan.

book_ref.quote: Similar to LIGO, there is another facility for measuring gravitational waves.

blocks.prompt: 24 The first gravitational waves observed travelled for 1.3 billion years at the speed of light, and the Virgo cluster is 50 million light years away. Taking 1 light year = 9.46 × 10¹² km, find (i) the distance travelled by those waves (ii) the distance of the Virgo cluster, both in km. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Waves moving at the speed of light for N years cover N light years; multiply by the km in one light year.

book_ref.quote: It took 1.3 billion years for the waves to arrive at the LIGO detector
